metaDescription: Six folding stove splatter guards compared: three and four panel shields, a pair of two-panel boards and a coated black model, with notes on size and cleanup.
introParagraphs: A stove splatter guard is not the same thing as a screen that sits on a pan. It is a freestanding shield, usually a set of hinged stainless panels, that stands behind and beside your cookware and catches grease before it reaches the wall, the cabinets and the countertop. Cooks reach for one when the mess is wider than a single pan can control: a crowded stovetop, a backsplash that is hard to scrub, or a wall behind the range that is painted rather than tiled.

The six guards here fall into three shapes. The Tylulikaty, MMUK and LTSEAME are four panel shields that wrap three sides of the cooking area. The CJFNDFA is a three panel guard with rounded corners and sealed edges. The LhyBtm comes as a pair of two panel boards you can arrange yourself, and the Baetle is a heavy-duty black powder coated shield whose listing gives exact panel dimensions.

We evaluated them from listing dimensions, materials and recurring buyer feedback, without claiming hands-on testing. The key questions are whether the panels reach high enough and wide enough for your stove, how the edges are finished, how flat the guard folds, and how much grease the surface holds. The sections below sort the models by those practical differences.

products.name: Baetle Foldable Stove Top Splatter Guard
products.description:
The Baetle guard is the model to pick when you want a shield that feels like a piece of equipment, not a foil screen. The listing states a 29.5 inch wide back panel when open, with 13.6 inch side panels, and it asks buyers outright to check size before ordering, which is a refreshingly honest note. The steel is described as thick and heat resistant, finished in black powder coat to reduce glare and hide the first signs of splashes.

The edges get serious attention. Closed hems and protective base strips are listed to make it safer to handle and to protect the surface it stands on, and both matter in a kitchen where you slide the guard around a hot stove. A black finish also looks less stark than raw stainless, though it will show dried grease marks in strong light and benefits from a wipe after each use.

Compared with the four-panel Tylulikaty and MMUK shields, the Baetle trades some adjustability for a sturdier build and an exact set of numbers you can measure your range against. It is the most fully described guard in this group, so it carries the least risk of an unpleasant surprise when it arrives. The listed 29.5 inch back panel is a sensible width for a standard cooktop, but check against your own stove, because the fit depends on your burners, not the label.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a sturdy, clearly measured shield for a standard cooktop.
pros: Exact panel dimensions in the listing
Black powder coat hides light staining
cons: Black finish shows dried grease in bright light
Fixed panel sizes may not suit narrow stoves

products.name: LTSEAME Large 4 Sided Stove Splatter Guard
products.description:
The LTSEAME guard is built around one idea: grease should wipe off. The listing says the surface carries a durable non-stick coating so oil stains come off with a damp cloth or a rinse, and the panels fold flat for storage. It is sold in black and in silver stainless looks, and the two are the same design, so choose by how much you mind seeing marks on your kitchen wall.

The maker also describes a full edge-folding method and an added black rubber strip to protect hands from scratches. Sharp sheet metal edges are a real concern with any bendable shield, so a finished edge and a soft strip are features worth noticing. The four sided layout wraps the back and both sides of the cooking area, which keeps splashes from escaping to the side as well as behind the pan.

Coatings are a mixed blessing. They make routine cleanup easy, but a scratched or scuffed non-stick layer is harder to repair than bare stainless, so skip abrasive pads and keep the guard away from sharp utensils. Compared with the Tylulikaty, which is galvanized sheet, this one puts its money into surface finish and edge safety. If you cook greasy food every day and want the quickest wipe-down, it is the strongest pick here.
products.bestFor: Daily frying where quick wipe-down matters most.
pros: Non-stick surface wipes with a damp cloth
Four sided coverage on three sides
cons: Panel dimensions are less detailed in the listing

products.description:
The Tylulikaty is the most spread-out guard in the lineup. The listing gives its size as 30 inches long, 11.4 inches wide and 12 inches high, and the four panels fold into different lengths, so you can open it to wrap a wide range or close it partway for a single burner. That adjustability is the real selling point, since a fixed shape fits only some stoves.

The material is stated as galvanized sheet, a zinc-coated steel that resists rust but behaves differently from stainless over years of heat and moisture. It is fine for a budget-conscious setup, and it stores flat in a drawer or against a wall. The listing frames it as protection for walls, counters and the cooking area, with the idea that you open it and set it around the pan.

Compared with the Baetle, you get more flexible geometry and a larger overall footprint, but less certainty about steel thickness and finish. Compared with the MMUK, the two share the four panel idea, so the choice often comes down to which listing gives the dimensions you can check against your stove. Measure before you buy and think of it as a flexible barrier for a wide cooking zone.
products.bestFor: Wide cooktops or two-burner frying where a flexible, large guard helps.
pros: Listed at 30 inches long and 12 high
Four panels wrap the cooking area

products.name: MMUK 4 Sided Stainless Splatter Guard for Stove
products.description:
The MMUK guard is a straightforward four sided stainless steel shield with an emphasis on folding quickly. The listing says it can be folded flat in seconds so you can store it easily, and that the stainless surface is easy to clean once the splashes dry. In the kitchen that means you can put it away right after cooking instead of leaving a bulky screen on the counter.

Stainless has the advantage of being familiar and durable: it does not coat, it does not flake, and it takes ordinary dish soap and a soft cloth. It is also the material most people already trust near heat. The tradeoff is that bare stainless shows fingerprints and water spots, and baked-on oil on its surface needs a little soaking rather than a one-pass wipe.

The listing is lighter on exact dimensions than the Baetle, so you should confirm the sizes on the product page before relying on it for a particular range. Compared with the LTSEAME, the MMUK gives up the coated surface for plain metal, and compared with the CJFNDFA it adds a fourth panel for extra side coverage. For many kitchens that makes it a balanced, middle-of-the-road choice.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a classic stainless four panel shield that folds away quickly.
pros: Stainless surface cleans with soap and cloth
cons: Dimensions are less detailed in the listing

products.name: CJFNDFA 3 Sided Stainless Splatter Guard
products.description:
The CJFNDFA is a three panel stainless guard that puts its attention on how the edges feel. The listing describes smooth, rounded corners and sealed hem edges, which reduces the chance of scratching your hands or marking the surfaces it touches. The material is high-grade stainless steel with a fine brushed finish, a surface that hides small scuffs better than a mirror polish.

Three panels make a simpler shape than four: a back and two sides. That is enough for most single-pan frying and takes less counter space. The listing says it contains grease splatter from the pan and calls the steel rust resistant, which suits a tool that lives near steam and wet cloths.

The lighter design means a bit less wraparound coverage than the four panel models. Where the Tylulikaty and MMUK add an extra panel, this one stays compact and easy to move. If you cook for one or two people and mostly use a single burner, the CJFNDFA gives you a neat, safe-feeling edge finish with less bulk to store. Compared with the LhyBtm boards, it is a single hinged unit and it will not break into separate pieces you can arrange yourself.
products.bestFor: Single-burner cooking where safe, rounded edges matter.
cons: Fewer panels mean less side coverage

products.name: LhyBtm 2 Pack Foldable Stainless Splatter Guard
products.description:
The LhyBtm is sold as a pack of two, with each guard a two sided foldable board made from 304 stainless steel. That gives you something other guards here cannot: you can set one behind the pan and the second to the side, or use one guard at a time and keep the other for a second burner. The listing calls it high temperature resistant and corrosion and rust resistant.

The maker also points out a heat insulation effect, saying it can keep plastics, spice jars and cans from being heated or deformed by the stove. That is a secondary benefit, and the practical advice is still to keep flammable or meltable things away from the cooktop altogether. As a splash barrier, the two small boards give you flexible placement but less wraparound structure than a single four panel unit, since each board stands on its own.

Placement matters with a pair. You need to stand them so they do not tip, and a full wrap takes some arranging. If you like reconfiguring, or want a barrier for the corner of a kitchen island, the two pack is a good fit. If you want one hinged shape that you open and set down, the CJFNDFA or the MMUK is quicker to use.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want two small barriers they can place around the stove as needed.
pros: Flexible placement behind or beside the pan
cons: Boards do not lock into one wrap
Less side coverage than a four panel unit

buyingCriteria.explanation: A stove guard only helps if it reaches high and wide enough to intercept the spray arc. Grease flies up and outward, so a guard that is shorter than about a foot lets droplets pass over the top. The Tylulikaty lists 12 inches of height, while the Baetle lists a 29.5 inch back panel with 13.6 inch side panels, so measure the width of your cooktop and the distance to the nearest wall before you buy. If you only fry on one burner, a smaller guard like the CJFNDFA is enough.

Three panels give a back and two sides, which suits single-burner cooking. Four panels, as on the Tylulikaty, MMUK and LTSEAME, add flexibility to wrap a wider area or to angle toward a corner. Two sided boards like the LhyBtm give maximum placement freedom but need arranging. Think about how you cook: one pan at a time or two. More panels also means more hinges to wipe and more bulk to store.

Stainless steel is the usual choice because it resists rust and takes soap and water. Galvanized sheet, as in the Tylulikaty listing, is zinc-coated steel and can be fine but is less standard near steam. Coated or powder-coated finishes, as on the LTSEAME and Baetle, wipe cleaner but should be washed without abrasive pads. A brushed finish, like the CJFNDFA, hides scuffs better than a mirror shine.

Thin folded metal can have sharp edges, and you will handle a stove guard with one hand while the stove is warm. Look for closed hems, rounded corners and edge strips. The CJFNDFA lists rounded corners and sealed hems, the Baetle lists closed hems with base strips, and the LTSEAME adds a rubber strip along folded edges. These details make daily handling noticeably safer.

A guard sits close to a hot pan and sometimes close to an open flame, so give the burner room. Keep the panels a few inches back from gas flames and make sure the guard does not block ventilation or trap heat against the wall. Coated and powder-coated finishes should not be pushed directly against a flame. The LhyBtm listing notes it can help insulate items from heat, but the safest approach is still to keep anything meltable off the cooktop.

The point of a foldable guard is that it can disappear after cooking. Check how thick it is when closed, because stacked panels with rubber strips and hems take more depth than a plain folded sheet. The MMUK emphasizes folding flat in seconds, and the LTSEAME and Tylulikaty also store flat. If your drawer is narrow, look at the listed length when folded rather than just the open size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint and coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated dimensions and panel counts to estimate how much of a typical cooktop each guard wraps. The Baetle and Tylulikaty give the most detailed numbers, while the four panel MMUK and LTSEAME offer similar layouts. Models with vague dimensions were scored more cautiously.

howWeEvaluated.title: Edge and handling safety
howWeEvaluated.description: Hemmed edges, rounded corners and rubber strips were weighted heavily because sheet metal guards are handled constantly. The CJFNDFA, Baetle and LTSEAME lead here. Listings that mention nothing about edge finishing earned less credit on this criterion.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material and rust resistance
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at whether the listing names stainless steel, galvanized sheet or a coated finish. The LhyBtm lists 304 stainless, the CJFNDFA lists high-grade stainless with a brushed finish, and the Tylulikaty lists galvanized sheet. Rust resistance matters because a guard lives near steam and wet cloths.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup and surface
howWeEvaluated.description: Wipe-down ease was assessed from the surface type: coated, brushed or plain stainless. The LTSEAME promotes a non-stick coat, and the stainless models rely on soap and a soft cloth. A surface that cleans in seconds is one you will actually clean.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: Within this group, the Baetle leads on documented build, the LTSEAME on wipe-down, the Tylulikaty on footprint, the MMUK on quick folding, the CJFNDFA on edge finish and the LhyBtm on placement flexibility. We did not rank them on a single scale because the right pick depends on your stove.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stove splatter guard and a splatter screen?
faq.a: A splatter screen sits on top of a single pan and blocks spray from above. A stove splatter guard is a freestanding shield that stands behind and beside the pan to protect the wall and counter. Screens control steam better, while guards cover a wider area. Many cooks use both for greasy jobs.

faq.q: How tall should a stove splatter guard be?
faq.a: Aim for at least about a foot, since grease often arcs upward before it falls. The Tylulikaty is listed at 12 inches high, which is a sensible height for stovetop frying. A shorter guard may stop spray from the sides but let droplets pass over the top. Measure the space between your cooktop and any shelf or hood.

faq.q: Is it safe to use a guard next to a gas flame?
faq.a: Keep the panels a few inches away from the flame and make sure the guard does not block burner air or trap heat against the wall. Coated or powder-coated surfaces should not be pressed against a flame. If you smell anything hot or see discoloration, move the guard back. Always let it cool before folding and storing.

faq.q: How do I clean a coated guard without damaging it?
faq.a: Use warm water, mild dish soap and a soft cloth or sponge. Avoid steel wool and abrasive powders, which can scratch the finish on models like the LTSEAME and Baetle. Wipe the panels after each use and dry the hinges so they stay free of rust. A quick routine prevents grease from baking on.

faq.q: Will a guard fit my small stove?
faq.a: Check the folded and open dimensions in the listing and compare them to your cooktop width. Small stoves do well with a three panel guard such as the CJFNDFA or a pair of two sided boards like the LhyBtm. Large four panel guards can crowd a narrow range and block access to controls. When in doubt, close the panels partway.

faq.q: Do stove guards replace wiping the wall?
faq.a: They reduce the amount of grease that lands on surfaces, but they do not eliminate it. You will still get a light film from steam, so occasional wiping is normal. A guard mainly keeps the heavy splatter off and makes the cleanup you do much easier.
